source.title: Benign Fine-Tuning Breaks Safety Alignment in Audio LLMs
source.authors: Jaechul Roh; Virat Shejwalkar; Amir Houmansadr

page_placements.theme: Runtime instructions, demonstrations and steering modulate safety

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether benign fine-tuning raises harmful-response rates in a new setting—audio LLMs—using LoRA fine-tuning and JSR evaluation; it also varies modality, datasets, and proximity filters.
record.gate_note: Tests V2 only. It measures harmful-response rates after benign fine-tuning, including random and proximity-filtered audio data. It does not test harmful-example fine-tuning, per-token KL concentration, compliant-opening or adversarial-suffix bypasses, localization in a small set of weights, or methods for deepening safety. Mechanistic refusal-direction measurements are not first-token measurements. Cited findings from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: It measures whether fine-tuning on benign audio data raises harmful compliance (HarmBench-classified JSR on AdvBench and SafetyBench) in three audio LLMs. It compares random and proximity-selected benign data against the pretrained baseline. This is V2 in a new setting, audio LLMs with frozen encoders and LoRA.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude benign audio fine-tuning raises JSR from single digits to up to 87.12%. The most damaging proximity axis (semantic, mixed or acoustic) depends on encoder/projector architecture. They attribute the degradation to late-layer refusal suppression with frozen encoders preserved, a recognition-refusal dissociation. This dissociation is inferred from refusal-direction projections; detection is not measured separately. Of the two defenses, the system prompt reduces JSR to near zero in all three models. Distant filtering helps AF3 and mostly Kimi but not Qwen2.5-Omni, despite the conclusion's blanket wording.
record.recipe_differences: Uses benign fine-tuning and harmful-prompt refusal/compliance evaluation, but applies them to audio LLMs with LoRA, proximity-selected audio datasets, and JSR classified by HarmBench rather than reproducing the text-model setup. This study is an extension to audio and architecture-dependent proximity axes.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with model architecture, proximity encoder/filtering axis, selected fraction, benign dataset, input modality, benchmark, and audio perturbation. The paper reports further variation by reasoning-oriented training data and system-prompt defense.

fits_no_version.finding: Audio fine-tuning collapses the late-layer (L20-26) projection onto a refusal direction at the last input token, tracking JSR. In AF3, text fine-tuning on the same samples preserves it (Figs. 3-4, App. A).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign fine-tuning degrades safety by suppressing a late-layer refusal direction rather than altering harmful-content representations.

fits_no_version.finding: A safety system prompt at inference restores refusal in the most degraded checkpoints, to AdvBench JSR 0.00-0.58% (Table 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety eroded by benign fine-tuning is recoverable by inference-time safety instructions.

record.problems: Only three models are evaluated and all use Whisper-family encoders; harmful audio benchmarks use one TTS engine (gTTS). JSR uncertainty estimates are not reported. The refusal-direction analysis uses small complied subsets (40 for AF3 and 1 for Qwen2.5-Omni), as the authors note. The paper reports many results in tables, but additional results are not extracted here because of the 60-row cap.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row cap is reached. Omitted Table 2 SafetyBench rows; text-modality control results (Section 5.3, Figure 2); alternative benign datasets and MELD results (Appendix E, Tables 5–6); distant-filtering and system-prompt defenses (Table 3 and Table 7); audio-noise perturbation results (Table 9); and utility results (Table 8). These are not needed to cover the extracted SD-QA JSR results, but include further outcomes relevant to benign fine-tuning or its mitigation.

untested.parts: Text-only LLMs are untested. The only text arm is a transcript fine-tuning control inside the audio models (Fig. 2).
No per-token KL or position-wise analysis of aligned vs base models.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding-change bypasses. The system prompt is a defense.
LoRA is used, but no test of whether safety sits in few weights or ranks. The late-layer refusal-direction projection is not a parameter-localization test.
No test of whether data or the training objective causes token-depth shallowness.

missing.what: SafetyBench JSR under semantic, acoustic and mixed reference filtering (e.g., Kimi semantic 75% +0.00, AF3 acoustic all decreases, Qwen acoustic up to +21.40)
Text-transcript vs audio fine-tuning control: AF3 text fine-tuning lowers AdvBench JSR to 2.12% (audio raises it to 20.19%); Qwen text 16.35% vs audio 9.42%
Alternative benign datasets GC Accents and MMSU (Kimi MMSU mixed 71.15%; AF3 MMSU slight decreases; Qwen near baseline)
MELD reasoning-data fine-tuning: small AdvBench increases (≤ +0.96), SafetyBench decreases
Distant-filtered benign fine-tuning: AF3 decreases throughout; Qwen still increases (up to +17.89 SafetyBench); Kimi mixed
Noise-augmented semantic 25% fine-tuning on Kimi: café noise 0.96%, traffic noise 18.46% AdvBench

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The rows faithfully copy Tables 1-2 AdvBench/SafetyBench values, checked against the text. The reader's supports label included partial and absent rows (r24, r44, r45, r57, r60); these are moved to limits_scope. No uncertainty is reported; JSR is computed from single runs. All three models use Whisper-family encoders, and the harmful prompts come from a single TTS engine (gTTS), so the acoustic-axis results may partly reflect TTS style. The refusal direction rests on 40 (AF3) and 1 (Qwen) complied examples.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and whether a few to a few hundred harmful examples remove refusal.

No test of benign fine-tuning in text-only LLMs; the study tests audio fine-tuning and a limited text-modality control. It does not establish that benign fine-tuning generally raises compliance across models or settings.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across response positions.
Compliant-token prefilling, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as bypasses. The safety system prompt is a defense, not a compliant opening bypass.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour; LoRA is used, but no such localization test is reported.
Whether data or training objectives produce first-token shallowness.
Training to spread safety beyond initial response tokens and testing whether that persists.

relationships.condition: SD-QA audio fine-tuning, all three models: model-internal filtering, most random-sampling cells, semantic and mixed filtering (AF3, Kimi 25%), and acoustic filtering for Qwen2.5-Omni and Kimi at 25%/75%
relationships.reason: JSR rises well above single-digit baselines, up to 58.08% (internal, r04) and 87.12% (semantic, r37). Random sampling also raises JSR in AF3 and Qwen (r13-r15, r19-r21, r25-r27, r31-r33).
relationships.display_finding: Jailbreak success rose well above single-digit baselines, reaching 58.08% with model-internal filtering and 87.12% with semantic filtering; random sampling also raised it for AF3 and Qwen.

relationships.condition: Kimi-Audio with random sampling at 25-50% of SD-QA
relationships.reason: Random benign fine-tuning barely moves or lowers JSR (AdvBench 5.38%, 2.88% vs 4.62%; SafetyBench 12.78%, 12.46% vs 14.16%) (r01, r02, r07, r08). Only the 75% fraction raises it (r03, r09).
relationships.display_finding: For Kimi-Audio, random benign fine-tuning on 25–50% of SD-QA barely moved or lowered JSR (AdvBench 5.38% and 2.88% vs 4.62%; SafetyBench 12.78% and 12.46% vs 14.16%); only the 75% fraction raised it.

relationships.condition: Dependence on the selection axis and fraction: AF3 acoustic (WavLM) filtering, Kimi acoustic/mixed at 50-75%, Qwen semantic/acoustic at 75%, AF3 internal 75% SafetyBench
relationships.reason: AF3 acoustic-filtered data lowers JSR at every fraction (2.88-3.65% vs 7.69%; r49-r51). Kimi acoustic 50% drops to 1.54% (r41), and Kimi mixed 50%/75% is near baseline (r44, r45). Qwen 75% cells rise only about 2 points (r57, r60), as does AF3 internal 75% SafetyBench (r24).
relationships.display_finding: AF3 acoustic-filtered data lowered JSR at every fraction (2.88–3.65% vs 7.69%), Kimi acoustic 50% fell to 1.54%, Kimi mixed 50% and 75% stayed near baseline, and Qwen at 75% and AF3 internal 75% on SafetyBench rose only about 2 points. Kimi acoustic 75%, however, raised AdvBench JSR to 19.23%.
